messages.content:
Assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category. Here are worked examples, then the case to code.

Example 1
Hospital course: A 72-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history was admitted with three days of worsening breathlessness and purulent sputum. Spirometry showed an FEV1/FVC ratio of 0.52. He was treated with nebulised bronchodilators, oral prednisolone and antibiotics for an infective exacerbation of his long-standing airflow limitation.
Answer: J44

Example 2
Hospital course: A 58-year-old man presented with crushing central chest pain radiating to the jaw. The electrocardiogram showed ST elevation in the anterior leads and high-sensitivity troponin rose from 40 to 2100 ng/L. He underwent primary percutaneous coronary intervention with a stent to the proximal left anterior descending artery.
Answer: I21

Example 3
Hospital course: A 34-year-old woman presented with fever, rigors, dysuria and right flank tenderness. Urine microscopy showed pyuria and culture grew Escherichia coli. Computed tomography showed a swollen right kidney with no abscess. She improved on intravenous ceftriaxone.
Answer: N10

Example 4
Hospital course: An 81-year-old woman was brought in after a fall at home. She could not weight-bear and the right leg was shortened and externally rotated. A pelvic radiograph showed a displaced subcapital fracture of the right femoral neck. She underwent hemiarthroplasty on day one.
Answer: S72

Example 5
Hospital course: A 19-year-old man presented with 18 hours of periumbilical pain that migrated to the right iliac fossa, with anorexia and a low-grade fever. There was guarding at McBurney's point and the white cell count was 15.2. Laparoscopy confirmed an inflamed, non-perforated appendix.
Answer: K35

Example 6
Hospital course: A 64-year-old woman with a history of oestrogen-receptor-positive breast carcinoma treated five years earlier presented with progressive thoracic back pain. Magnetic resonance imaging showed deposits in T7 and T9 with no cord compression. Biopsy confirmed deposits of breast origin and she received palliative radiotherapy to the spine.
Answer: C79

Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

Hospital Course:
The patient presented to the pediatric emergency with confusion and disorientation. She was diagnosed with bacterial meningitis based on clinical examination and CSF analysis and was treated with intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin. A CT scan was performed, and pneumocephalus was observed in the right frontal region. The patient was treated for signs of chronic sinusitis and pansinusitis. She showed initial symptomatic improvements to antibiotics but suffered a deterioration of her GCS to 7/15, with a high-grade fever.

Subdural empyema was diagnosed through a repeat CT scan, requiring immediate neurosurgical intervention. The surgical drainage was performed, and on the second day, the patient's GCS improved to 15/15, and her fever had subsided. The patient was discharged with a prescription for oral antibiotics, nasal saline spray, and nasal decongestants.
Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Treatment:
The patient received intravenous ceftriaxone and vancomycin to treat bacterial meningitis. Subdural empyema was treated through immediate neurosurgical intervention, which involved surgical drainage. The patient was prescribed oral antibiotics, nasal saline spray, and nasal decongestants upon discharge.

Follow-up:
The patient was seen at two-week and four-week follow-ups and experienced significant improvements in symptoms.

Answer with the three-character category only.

text:
The main condition treated was bacterial meningitis, with subdural empyema as a complication. The empyema came from sinusitis and needed surgical drainage.

In ICD-10-AM, intracranial abscess and granuloma are coded to G06 (intracranial and intraspinal abscess and granuloma), which includes subdural empyema (G06.2 is extradural and subdural abscess). Bacterial meningitis is coded to G00. Both were present on admission.

Choosing the principal diagnosis is the hard part. The patient was admitted with meningitis, but the subdural empyema was the condition that required the major treatment, neurosurgical drainage. The empyema was probably already present at admission, since pneumocephalus was seen on the first CT, and it was diagnosed later. G00 carries an Excludes note for meningitis in bacterial diseases classified elsewhere. There is also a G07 code, "intracranial and intraspinal abscess and granuloma in diseases classified elsewhere," but it does not apply here.

The meningitis was the reason for presentation and was treated first, while the empyema was a later finding that drove the surgery. Under the principal diagnosis definition (the condition chiefly responsible for the episode of care), G06 has a reasonable case, since the surgery was the main resource use and the meningitis was likely secondary to the sinus infection and empyema. Even so, the presenting and first-treated condition was bacterial meningitis, so I will choose G00.

**G00**
